content_html:
Discount points are an upfront fee you pay your lender at closing in exchange for a lower interest rate. One point costs 1% of the loan amount. Whether points are worth buying depends on how long you keep the loan: the savings arrive a little each month, while the cost is paid all at once. This calculator finds the break-even point and your net gain or loss over the years you expect to keep the mortgage.

How to use this calculator

  1. Loan amount and term: the amount you are borrowing and the repayment period.
  2. Rate with no points and rate with points: take both from the same lender's quote so they are comparable. Fractions of a point are fine, such as 0.5 or 1.25.
  3. Points: the number of points you would buy.
  4. Years you expect to keep the loan: until you would sell or refinance.
  5. Return on cash (optional): what the money could earn if you kept it instead, for example in savings. Leave it at 0 to ignore this.

Two ways to measure break-even

The simple break-even divides the cost of the points by the monthly payment saving. It is quick, but it ignores the fact that a lower rate also pays your balance down faster.

The full break-even, shown as the main result, adds that extra equity. After each month it compares your payment savings so far plus the difference in loan balances with the cost of the points. Once that total turns positive, the points have paid for themselves. If you enter a return on cash, the cost of the points and the savings are both grown at that rate, so the points have to beat what the money could have earned elsewhere.

Worked example

On a $300,000, 30-year loan, a lender offers 6.75% with no points or 6.375% for 1.5 points:

ItemResult
Cost of 1.5 points$4,500.00
Monthly payment, no points / with points$1,945.79 / $1,871.61
Monthly saving$74.18
Simple break-even5 years 1 month
Full break-even, counting extra equity4 years
Net gain if you keep the loan 10 years$6,779.30

Kept for all 30 years, the lower rate saves $26,706.45 in interest, or $22,206.45 after the cost of the points. If the cash could otherwise earn 4% a year, break-even moves out to 4 years 6 months.

Tips before you buy points

  • Be realistic about how long you will keep the loan. Many people refinance or move sooner than they expect, and points paid on a loan you end early are mostly lost.
  • Ask for quotes with and without points on the same day, since rates change daily.
  • Compare the extra cash needed at closing with your emergency savings. A bigger down payment or cash reserve can matter more than a slightly lower rate.
  • Points on a mortgage for your main home may be tax deductible. Check IRS Publication 936 or ask a tax professional.

faq.question: How much does one mortgage point cost?
faq.answer: One point costs 1% of the loan amount. On a $300,000 loan, one point is $3,000 and half a point is $1,500.

faq.question: How much does a point lower my rate?
faq.answer: It varies by lender and by day. A reduction of around a quarter of a percentage point per point is often quoted, but always compare actual quotes.

faq.question: What is the difference between discount points and origination points?
faq.answer: Discount points buy a lower interest rate. Origination points are a fee for processing the loan and do not reduce the rate.

faq.question: Why does the full break-even come sooner than the simple one?
faq.answer: A lower rate means more of each payment goes to principal, so you owe less at any point in time. Counting that extra equity makes the points pay off sooner.

faq.question: Should I buy points if I might refinance soon?
faq.answer: Usually not. If you refinance before the break-even point, the money spent on points will have cost more than it saved.
